------------------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY

Strategy: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension (Sun & Abraham, 2021) and an additional “difference-in-difference-in-differences” (DDD) interaction to capture the moderating role of regulation.

Rationale
• Between 2000-2006 a number of countries enacted corporate-governance reforms that forced banks to increase board independence, limit insider lending, or raise disclosure standards (e.g., Germany’s KonTraG amendment 2002, Italy’s “Draghi” and “Patto Chiaro” laws, Korea’s 2001 outside-director rule). These reforms were externally imposed and sharply timed, providing quasi-experimental variation in governance.
• Adoption timing differs by country → staggered rollout fits DID well.
• The research question explicitly asks how regulation shapes the governance–risk link, so we interact the DID treatment with a continuous index of regulatory stringency (e.g., Barth-Caprio-Levine “BankReg” index). This yields a DDD coefficient measuring whether the same reform reduces risk more where prudential rules are tight.
• Panel structure (banks × year) lets us difference out time-invariant bank heterogeneity and common macro shocks using two-way fixed effects.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL

Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for bank i operating in country c in year t ≥ τ_c, where τ_c is the first fiscal year after country c’s governance reform becomes binding. Governance reform is defined as any statute or binding regulation that (i) mandates ≥ x% independent directors on bank boards or (ii) caps the voting rights of controlling shareholders (threshold x chosen following Bebchuk & Weisbach 2010; we will document sources in an appendix).

Control group  
(a) Banks in the same country in pre-reform years.  
(b) Banks in countries that have not yet reformed by t (“not-yet-treated”) serve as additional contemporaneous controls.

Treatment timing / event date  
τ_c is coded as the first full fiscal year after the reform’s enactment. We will confirm the exact effective dates in country legislation; if a reform in Nov-2002 affects fiscal-year-2003 statements, τ_c = 2003.

Running variable & cutoff  
Not applicable (not an RDD).

Variable for regulatory environment  
Reg_c,t = standardized index of capital-regulation stringency, prompt-corrective-action powers, and supervisor independence from Barth, Caprio & Levine (2006). Higher values = stricter.

DDD specification  
Treated_c,t × Post_c,t × Reg_c,t captures how regulation amplifies (or dampens) the reform effect.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS

A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of reform, risk-taking trends for banks in reforming vs. never/late-reforming countries would have moved in parallel.  
Plausibility: Pre-reform macro conditions were similar across OECD and large emerging markets in 2000-01. We will test visually and formally via event-study leads (-5 to -1 years).

A2. Exogeneity of Reform Timing: The exact year a country enacts governance rules is unrelated to latent, country-specific changes in bank risk that would have occurred anyway.  
Plausibility: Many reforms were responses to internationally driven initiatives (Basel, OECD CG Principles) or scandals in non-bank sectors, reducing reverse causality. We will reinforce with country-specific pre-trends controls and propensity-score re-weighting.

A3. No Interference (Stable Unit Treatment Value): A reform in country c does not instantly change the risk of banks in country d that has not yet reformed (no cross-border contagion).  
Plausibility: Most banks operate domestically under home regulation; we drop multinational branches where booking centers might blur treatment.

A4. Stable Composition: Entry/exit around reforms is not differentially related to latent risk.  
Plausibility: Short time window; we will include bank-fixed effects and show attrition balance.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION

Threat 1: Endogenous Reform Adoption  
• Mitigation: (i) Include country-specific linear and quadratic time trends.  
(ii) Instrumental-variable robustness: instrument Treat × Post with an indicator for whether the country is in a Legal-Origin family whose corporate-law reforms are synchronized (e.g., EU directives implementation deadlines).

Threat 2: Anticipation or Delayed Compliance  
Banks may adjust risk before law becomes binding or gradually after.  
• Mitigation: Event-study with ± 5 leads and lags; re-define Post as year ≥ τ_c + 1 and show robustness when excluding the transition year.

Threat 3: Concurrent Banking Crises or Macro Shocks  
A crisis can coincide with reforms, biasing estimates.  
• Mitigation: Control for country-year macro variables (GDP growth, inflation, global liquidity) and interact them with region dummies; use country-year fixed effects in a robustness “within-country” specification.

5. R CODE OUTLINE

```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data work
library(fixest)       # panel estimations
library(did)          # Sun & Abraham implementation
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# -------------------------------------------------
banks   <- fread("bank_financials.csv")        # risk, controls
gov     <- fread("governance_reforms.csv")     # τ_c
reg     <- fread("regulatory_index.csv")       # Reg_c,t

# merge
data <- merge(banks, gov,   by = c("country"))
data <- merge(data,  reg,   by = c("country","year"))

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# -------------------------------------------------
# Risk-taking proxy: std deviation of ROA over past 3 yrs
data[, roa_SD := frollapply(ROA, 3, sd, align = "right"), by = bank_id]

# Treatment status & timing
data[, post := as.integer(year >= reform_year)]
data[, treated := as.integer(!is.na(reform_year))]
data[, time_to_event := year - reform_year]    # for event study
data[, treat_post := treated*post]

# DDD interaction
data[, DDD := treat_post * Reg_Index]

# Bank & country fixed effect identifiers
data[, bank_fe := factor(bank_id)]
data[, ctry_year := interaction(country, year, drop = TRUE)]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Specification (TWFE Sun&Abraham)
# -------------------------------------------------
# Convert to factor for did
data[, treat_year := ifelse(treated==1, reform_year, 0)]

sa_res <- sunab(data$treat_year, data$year)

model_main <- feols(
  roa_SD ~ sunab(reform_year, year) + Reg_Index + 
           sunab(reform_year, year):Reg_Index | 
           bank_id + year, 
  cluster = ~country, data = data
)

etable(model_main)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. DDD Specification
# -------------------------------------------------
model_DDD <- feols(
  roa_SD ~ treat_post + DDD + bank_controls + macro_controls | 
           bank_id + year , 
  cluster = ~country, data = data
)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness Check: Stacked DID (Callaway & Sant’Anna)
# -------------------------------------------------
cs <- did::att_gt(
  yname   = "roa_SD",
  tname   = "year",
  idname  = "bank_id",
  gname   = "reform_year",
  xformla = ~ bank_controls + Reg_Index,
  data    = data,
  panel   = TRUE,
  est_method = "dr"
)
did::aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")  # dynamic effects

# -------------------------------------------------
# 6. Save results
# -------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(list(main=model_main, DDD=model_DDD, cs=cs), "results.Rds")
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS

Theory predicts that stronger internal governance (more independent directors, limits on controlling shareholders) curbs managerial risk-shifting and thus lowers risk-taking measures. I expect:

• Average reduction in risk-taking of roughly 0.3–0.5 standard-deviations of the dependent variable after a reform.  
• Interaction: Effect is 30–40 % larger (more negative) when the regulatory-stringency index is one SD above the mean (consistent with complementarity between internal and external discipline).

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)

C1: Parallel trends supported by pre-trend tests → 1  
C2: No interference across units (geographic isolation of treatment) → 0.8  
C3: No simultaneous confounders (controlled with FE & macro vars) → 0.7  
C4: Correct model for staggered adoption (Sun-Abraham / Callaway-Sant’Anna) → 1  
C5: Robust standard errors & clustering at treatment level → 1  

Average score ≈ 0.9 → identification reasonably credible, but still subject to reform endogeneity concerns highlighted above.

------------------------------------------------------------
